explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. The disciples are together with the doors locked for fear of the Jews, and Jesus came and stood among them anyway. The text doesn't tell us how He got in, so I'm not going to guess. I just know a locked door was no problem for Him.

Close, but the text says something different. The doors are locked for fear of the Jews, and still “Jesus came and stood among them.” A locked door doesn't keep Him out. The disciples got a visitor they weren't expecting, that's for sure.

That's the one. After He greets them, Jesus shows the disciples His hands and His side. Those are where the nails and the wound were, and Thomas will bring them up again in a bit. Stay tuned, because that detail matters later.

explanations.answer: The linen cloths from the tomb
explanations.explanation: Linen cloths do show up in this chapter, but earlier. Peter, one of the disciples, looks into the tomb and sees them lying there (John 20:6). In the locked room, Jesus shows His hands and His side. I'd say the cloths were just left at the tomb.

No scroll comes out in this scene, friend. The text says Jesus shows them His hands and His side. That's all the disciples need to look at. I'd guess nobody in that room was thinking about reading material.

Yes, they rejoiced! The text says the disciples rejoiced when they saw the Lord. A minute earlier they were behind locked doors, and now there's joy in that room. I bet nobody was thinking about the doorbell anymore.
No arguing in this room, friend. The text says the disciples rejoiced when they saw the Lord. Nobody's debating anything once He shows them His hands and His side. It's a joyful moment.
I can see why you'd say it, with those locked doors. But the text doesn't say they trembled. It says the disciples rejoiced when they saw the Lord. I think the joy hit them fast.

Almost, but He says the opposite. Right after the second greeting of peace, Jesus says, “As the Father has sent Me, so also I am sending you.” Being sent means going out. Nobody gets sent out while staying behind a locked door.
Exactly right. Jesus doesn't say a word about staying put. He says, “As the Father has sent Me, so also I am sending you.” Those locked doors were about to have less to do with their day.

That's right. Jesus breathes on them and says, “Receive the Holy Spirit.” The Holy Spirit is God's own Spirit, and Jesus is the one giving this gift. I think that breath is a moment worth slowing down for.

Those keys are real, but they come up in a different place. Jesus tells Peter, one of the disciples, “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven…” (Matthew 16:19). In the locked room, the thing Jesus says to receive is the Holy Spirit. Don't mix up the key rings, friend.
No new name gets handed out in this scene, friend. After breathing on them, Jesus says, “Receive the Holy Spirit.” That's what He tells them to receive. Names can wait for another day.
That's the word. Jesus says, “If you forgive anyone his sins, they are forgiven…” It's a big thing to say to the disciples. I'd say they stood a little taller hearing it.
That's not the word Jesus uses, friend. He says, “If you forgive anyone his sins, they are forgiven…” The word is forgiven, plain and simple. Nothing about sins being remembered there.
Jesus doesn't say judged here. He says, “If you forgive anyone his sins, they are forgiven…” The sentence is about forgiveness from start to finish. Keep your gavel in the drawer, friend.

Not this time, friend. The other disciples tell Thomas, one of the Twelve, “We have seen the Lord!” But he replies, “…I will never believe.” That's a big no from him, at least until he sees for himself.
That's it. Thomas, one of the Twelve, hears the other disciples say, “We have seen the Lord!” Instead of believing right away, he says, “…I will never believe.” He wants more than their word.

explanations.answer: To see and touch His wounds
explanations.explanation: You've got it. Thomas says, “Unless I see the nail marks in His hands, and put my finger where the nails have been, and put my hand into His side, I will never believe.” He's very specific about it. Thomas knows exactly what he's asking for.

explanations.answer: To hear the Lord's own voice
explanations.explanation: Hearing His voice isn't on Thomas's list, friend. He says he needs to see the nail marks in His hands, put his finger where the nails have been, and put his hand into His side. That's what he asks for. It's all about the wounds.
The tomb isn't what Thomas asks for. He says he needs to see the nail marks in Jesus' hands and put his hand into His side. The tomb doesn't come up in his words. His mind is on the wounds.
That's the word. Jesus says, “Stop doubting and believe.” Thomas had said he would never believe, and now Jesus speaks right to that. It's a straight word from the Lord, and I think Thomas knew it.
Fear was in that room earlier, because the doors were locked for fear of the Jews. But this line is for Thomas, and Jesus says, “Stop doubting and believe.” He's speaking to what Thomas said, friend.
Waiting isn't the word here. Jesus says to Thomas, “Stop doubting and believe.” Thomas has already waited eight days. Now Jesus tells him to believe.
That's what Thomas says. “My Lord and my God!” After everything he said he needed, those are his words to Jesus. It's quite a thing for him to say out loud.
Thomas doesn't say that, friend. His words to Jesus are, “My Lord and my God!” Nothing about coming back. He goes straight to who Jesus is.

That cry belongs to someone else. Bartimaeus, a blind beggar, called out, “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!” (Mark 10:46-47). Thomas says something different here, “My Lord and my God!” Same Jesus, different moment.

Jesus actually says more than that. He tells Thomas, “Because you have seen Me, you have believed; blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed.” So the blessing also reaches those who haven't seen. That includes folks who weren't standing in that room.

Right! Jesus says, “…blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed.” So the blessing isn't only for people who saw Him. It reaches past that room, friend. That's good news for anybody who hasn't seen Him with their own eyes.

You got it, baker. The writer says Jesus performed many other signs in the presence of His disciples, and they are not written in this book. Not everything He did made it onto the page. It sure makes me curious what else there was.

The text says the opposite, friend. The writer says Jesus performed many other signs in the presence of His disciples, which are not written in this book. So there's more He did than what's on the page. The writer only included some.

explanations.answer: So you may believe and have life
explanations.explanation: That's the reason. The writer says these are written “so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in His name.” It's written for the one reading, and that means you. You've been baking right in the middle of it.

explanations.answer: So the temple keeps a record
explanations.explanation: The temple isn't mentioned in the writer's reason. He says these are written “so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God…” It's about believing, friend, not about keeping files.

The disciples are in the story, but that's not the reason given. The writer says these are written “so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in His name.” The goal is believing and life in His name. I'd say that's a better reason than a spot in the history books.
